doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: American Idol and young singers rushing into the business
summary: She worries about the pressures on young singers and urges early training and patience.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you think people try to do that before they’re ready, when they’re too young?

To do, to be — well I guess I’m thinking of — maybe I didn’t ask that right, but this phenomenon about American Idol and the over-use I believe of the term “diva” over the years. I wonder how that affects impressionable young aspiring people?

Yes. I understand the question. I watch American Idol. I watch it primarily because I work with young people. Some of it I don’t particularly care for but then that’s not me. You know, it’s not about me it’s about them. And I understand young people having that ambition and having that goal, but you’ve got to prepare for it. That’s a rough, rough business. And I’m not just talking about just musically. You’ve got to be prepared to take the rough edges, you know, the rough comments. You have to be prepared to cry, you know? You have to be prepared to accept some of the things that are going to come down the pike with that. Why? Because if you pursue this career you’re going to run into that same thing. You’re going to run into that same thing. Criticisms, people don’t like you, people will say things about you — true or untrue. People will do things to hurt you. They will do things to — how should I say, I don’t want to say, what’s the word — to keep you from being successful, out of jealousy, out of envy. You know, those kind of things, and you’ve got to be ready for that. And I think that some of our young people are not ready for that side of it. And so when I watch that program and I listen to the young people and I think that there are some demands being put on them that they’re not ready for. I wonder if after rehearsals if they can speak, you know? Because sometimes the demands are such that you’ve got to give me this big, big sound and we can do it over and over and over and over until you get it. Well, whew. I need a break. I need to be able to be quiet. I shouldn’t be hoarse when I finish singing. So I don’t know how they do it, you know, with the young people. I don’t know how much they demand of them. But I think that some of the material does not suit the singer. I really do.
That’s a good answer. It must be a little tricky sometimes when parents come to you also. Have they ever come and said, “Do you think my daughter should be pursuing a professional career in music?”

There are some, now in all honesty there are some young people, I mean you see it now, that they’re going to be a star. I mean you see it now. But they’re learning now. They’re getting the training now. They’re not waiting until they get 19, 20 and 21 to start the training. The training is starting at 9, 10, 11, 12. So that by the time they get of the age of majority, if you will, by the time they get there, they’ve had a lot of groundwork there. And so those are the ones who will be able to survive I think. But I don’t think it works very well when you’re 19 and you want to go on the stage at 19-1/2. Because they’re in a hurry. And you have to have patience in preparing for this. But many of them are in a hurry. You know they want to hurry up and get it so they can hurry up and do this or they
can hurry up and do that. You know, so they can hurry up. And when you get to the point where you can’t hurry anymore then what do you have to fall back on?
